copy.title: How do Moon phases change?
copy.tldr: The illuminated part of the Moon that we see changes as its position shifts relative to Earth and the Sun. In this simplified circular-orbit model, θ is the phase angle and f is the visible illuminated fraction from zero to one; sunlight is parallel and orbital tilt and eclipses are omitted.
copy.learning_objective: Connect the Moon's phase angle causally to its visible illuminated fraction.
copy.misconception: Moon phases are not caused by Earth's shadow, but by the Moon's position relative to Earth and the Sun.
copy.explanation_prompt: Move the phase angle, observe the visible illuminated fraction, and explain why it reaches zero at 0° and one at 180°.
copy.transfer_prompt: Use the relationship to find the visible illuminated fraction at 270°, then compare it with 90°.
suggestions: Explore how the angle of light changes shadow length.
Explore seasons as Earth's axial tilt changes.
Model solar and lunar eclipses by aligning the bodies.
copy.brief_summary: Shows how phase angle changes the Moon's visible illuminated fraction.
